A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAD constraint-generation study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original SketchGraphs experiments comparing constraint-generation models, including benchmark scores, diversity measurements, training curves, and failed approaches.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds sampling sensitivity results, a modified-reward experiment, dataset analyses, and a professional CAD designer preference study.

M1.justification: Appendix C.5 introduces an RLOO variant with two additional penalties: total constraints and dimensions normalized by entity count, and dimensions as a fraction of all generated constraints and dimensions. This is a targeted objective extension; the architecture, solver-feedback pipeline, and original algorithms remain.

E1.justification: The SketchGraphs corpus, CAD domain, and constraint-generation task remain unchanged. V2 adds a professional-designer evaluation population and a preference study using 30 sketches, a limited extension beyond automated evaluation.

E2.justification: The seven models compared in Tables 1 and 2 are unchanged. V2 adds reward-penalized RLOO to the evaluated alternatives; the new human study compares it with SFT, DPO, ExIt, and original RLOO.

E3.justification: V2 adds Pass@4 evaluation across temperatures 1.0/1.5 and top-p thresholds 0.5/1.0, plus a forced-choice study excluding unstable outputs. C.6 reports five designers, 30 sketches, and 1,500 judgments, although Figure C.4's 180-comparison instruction conflicts with the implied 300 judgments per participant. Existing benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendices C.4–C.6 examine sampling sensitivity, excessive dimension generation and reward penalties, and whether designers prefer the generated constraints. These substantially extend validation of robustness and design alignment. Earlier diversity analyses, iteration studies, training curves, and failed attempts remain.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains its eight-sample evaluation and standard-deviation reporting. V2 introduces no new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-training uncertainty procedures; the human study reports preference percentages without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, and C.1 retain their earlier scores. V2 adds constraint-type frequencies, sampling Pass@4 results, and reward-penalized RLOO results of 72.79% fully constrained and 82.83% stable. Table C.3 adds human preferences: ExIt beats original RLOO in 94% of comparisons, and penalized RLOO beats it in 92%.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds formal constraint-state definitions using Jacobian rank and residual rigid-body degrees of freedom, beyond v1's verbal descriptions. No proofs are added. The new over-constrained criterion, rank(J_C) > n-r, is problematic because redundant equations need not increase rank.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the design-alignment framing, solver-feedback approach, and headline 93% versus 34% and 8.9% fully-constrained results. Changing 'without alignment' to 'without SFT' clarifies the same baseline rather than changing the scientific claim.

C2.justification: V2 newly identifies dimension-based reward hacking in the successful RL models, extending beyond v1's failed-PPO discussion. It distinguishes high solver scores from designer preferences and explains the tradeoff between reduced dimensional locking and lower fully-constrained/stability scores. Appendix B.2 also adds a substantive rationale for functional evaluation instead of exact constraint matching.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the AWS instance, GPU memory, CPU count, and system memory, discloses random test-set selection for Figure 5, and adds a project-page link for additional results. The three-day runtime discussion is relocated to Appendix B.1, while existing training hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds two Hoffmann and Joan-Arinyo constraint-solving references supporting the formal definitions. The principal research positioning remains unchanged. Its additional Bouma bibliography entry duplicates a work already cited in v1 rather than introducing another distinct source.

P1.justification: V2 edits the solver and qualitative-results explanations, clarifies ExIt/DPO notation, subdivides the appendix, relocates runtime discussion, and updates the author list. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain, so the additions do not constitute extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figure 5 gains red input-geometry overlays that expose distortion directly. V2 also adds the stability illustration, preference chart, and study-interface screenshot; introduces sampling and preference tables; and expands Table A.2 with constraint-type distributions. These substantially extend the visual presentation of evidence.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's missing validation that solver success reflects design intent. Sections C.5–C.6 expose over-dimensioning, test a remedy, and establish strong designer preferences against original RLOO despite its leading solver scores. This materially improves empirical validity and interpretation. The small, stability-filtered study, inconsistent study reporting, and problematic new rank definition require correction, but do not outweigh that central gain.
